script: Dogs bark for a reason, so the first step in stopping barking is understanding why. Some dogs bark from excitement, some from boredom, some from fear, and some to get your attention. Yelling at a barking dog often makes things worse, because your dog thinks you are joining in. Start by removing the trigger when you can. If your dog barks at people walking past the window, close the blinds or move the furniture. Next, teach a quiet cue. Wait for a pause in the barking, say quiet in a calm voice, and reward the silence right away. Slowly increase the time between the cue and the treat. Third, meet your dog's needs. A tired, mentally stimulated dog barks less, so add a longer walk, some sniffing time, or a chew toy to the day. Fourth, do not reward attention barking. If your dog barks at you for food or play, wait for silence before you respond. Consistency is what makes this work. Everyone in the home should use the same rules, and progress comes in small steps. If barking is sudden or intense, check with your vet to rule out pain or anxiety.
